new_statements.translation: Besides the Toguchi dialect [Tatsugo], the Naze town dialect treated in §6.3, the Higashi-ku dialect of Yoron, and the Naze Ashikebu dialect of §7.2.2 are multi-pattern accent systems. [...] Overall, however, the Amami dialects are predominantly 'N-pattern', with 'multi-pattern' systems scattered among them (p. 45). [...] Traditionally the area of northern Amami Oshima from Kasari town to Tatsugo town was held to consist almost entirely of dialects with no accent oppositions. According to my survey, however, every dialect there has accent distinctions, created by the same change as in the Sani dialect (Uwano 1996b). In Yamato and Sumiyo villages in central Oshima, on the other hand, I was able to confirm that they really are one-pattern (accentless) (p. 50).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word prosody is lexical pitch accent, not stress, and it varies by village within the language: the northern (Kasari-Tatsugo-Naze) villages all have lexically contrastive pitch patterns, either N-pattern (a fixed small set of word-tone melodies, e.g. Sani's three patterns α 0「0(=) / β / γ 「0」0, with the α rising-then-level pattern taken by the overwhelming majority of 2+ mora words) or multi-pattern (Naze town, Toguchi, Ashikebu: locus of the pitch rise/fall or the register is lexically distinctive, an n+1-type system), while Yamato and Sumiyo villages are one-pattern (no lexical contrast). The Ura village sketch (Shigeno 2010: 18) likewise reports no lexically distinctive pitch, with a default low-then-high contour (LH, LHH..).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed (pitch accent description; no stress levels).
new_statements.exceptions: Uwano notes the accent contrasts in the Kasari-Tatsugo area are recent, arising from fusion of the first two morae or initial devoicing (tonogenesis), so pattern membership is unrelated to the Japanese accent classes and is very lopsided (Sani: pattern A overwhelmingly dominant). Contradicting first-hand report for one northern village: Shigeno 2010, Ura (Tatsugo), p. 18: 'Ura does not have lexically distinctive pitch. The default pitch pattern is LH for bimoraic words, LHH for trimoraic words, and so on.' Earlier surveys (Hattori et al. 1959; Hirayama et al. 1966) had called Sani and the north one-pattern.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation forms with and without one-mora particles nu/kara); accent unit is the word plus enclitics; units shorter than N morae show fewer than N contrasts. Statements are village-specific; the language-level reading 'pitch accent' summarizes Uwano's survey of the northern villages and is provisional.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog nort2935 = the North Oshima dialects (Amami City incl. Naze and Kasari, Tatsugo town, Yamato village; Sumiyo). The quoted Uwano 2000 statement covers Kasari, Tatsugo (Toguchi), Naze (town and Ashikebu), Yamato and Sumiyo; the Sani reports (Uwano 1996/1997) describe the Sani 'language island' at the northern tip of Kasari; Shigeno 2010 describes Ura village, Tatsugo. Note that Glottolog's reference list for nort2935 attaches the Shodon works (Martin 1970, Serafim 1984, Karimata 1996) although Shodon is on Kakeroma Island, Setouchi, which is Southern Amami-Oshima territory (sout2954), and Kato 2022, which describes Tokunoshima (toku1246). Karimata 1996a's Shodon acute/grave accent statement is therefore reported here but not used as the nort2935 statement.

tone_statements.citation: Hattori, Shirō 服部四郎 (author); Uwano, Zendo 上野善道 (annotations 補注). 2018. 日本祖語の再建 [The reconstruction of Proto-Japanese]. Tokyo: Iwanami Shoten 岩波書店. 666 pp. ISBN 978-4-00-061268-5. NDL R100000002-I028949989.
tone_statements.quote: There are three accentual distinctions in Naze dialect. They are atonic, penultimate accent, and final accent. No register distinction is involved. Atonic nouns have high pitch on the final mora of a 'prosodic word', e.g., hana LH 'nose', or hana-ga LL-H 'nose (Nom.)'. ... Penultimate-accent nouns have high pitch on the penultimate mora and the rest of each word is low in pitch, e.g., ha lri HL 'needle' ... With regard to Tone Bearing Units (TBU), the Naze TBU is the mora, because the pitch changes between moras within the same syllable, e.g., kagan LLH'mirror'.
tone_statements.summary: Naze (northern Amami Oshima): locus pitch accent with three distinctions, atonic, penultimate accent and final accent; no register contrast; the mora bears the tone; accent domain is the lexical word.

tone_statements.summary: One-pattern word melody (fixed pitch pattern per prosodic unit) in central Amami Ōshima, argued to be tonal not accentless.

sources.note: Abstract p. 1: Sani verb conclusive forms have two patterns (A, C); adjectives three (A, B, C); C pattern arose from initial voiceless morae or fusion of the first two morae; noun 3-pattern system recapitulated p. 2.

sources.citation: Karimata, Shigehisa かりまたしげひさ. 1996. 鹿児島県大島郡瀬戸内町諸鈍方言のフォネーム（上）. 日本東洋文化論集 1: 1-23. hdl:20.500.12000/2290.
sources.note: §1 (pp. 1-3): Shodon words are organized into feet of light/heavy syllables; each foot type shows a lexical opposition between two accent types, 'acute accent' (falling, pitch and intensity raised together) and 'grave accent' (rising), following Uemura's rhythm-accent framework; no CV-only words, weak/strong syllables alternate. (Shodon is on Kakeroma Island, Setouchi; Glottolog files it under nort2935.)

sources.citation: Uwano, Zendo 上野善道. 1996. 奄美大島佐仁方言のアクセント調査報告—名詞の部. 琉球の方言 20: 26-57. doi:10.15002/00012591.
sources.note: Abstract p. 26: Sani (Kasari), earlier reported as one-pattern (Hattori 1959) or 'one step short of one-pattern' (Hirayama et al. 1966: 127-130), is most likely a 3-pattern accent system; p. 30: 'clear accent oppositions are recognized' (speakers volunteer minimal pairs); p. 38: provisional conclusion 3-pattern (A, B, C) with heavily skewed membership, A overwhelmingly dominant, C arising from shortened/fused initial syllables.
